A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASGO. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including material moved from v1's main text into v2's appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original NanoGPT/Shakespeare training results and a query/key-processing ablation in Section 7 and Figures 3–4.

after.justification: V2 retains the NanoGPT experiments and adds GPT2 pretraining, GPT2-Large fine-tuning, and numerical sensitivity analyses in Section 7 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: Practical ASGO changes from fixed right-side preconditioning to choosing the smaller matrix dimension: left when m < n, right otherwise (Algorithm 2). This changes the update procedure for rectangular matrices, while the basic accumulated-gradient algorithm, DASGO, and head-wise query/key design remain.

E1.justification: Beyond retained Shakespeare character modeling, v2 adds GPT2 pretraining on OpenWebText and GPT2-Large fine-tuning on WikiText-2 with causal language modeling and fill-in-the-middle objectives. These substantially expand the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: The corresponding NanoGPT comparison retains AdamW, Shampoo, and Muon. New GPT2 experiments reuse AdamW and Muon; no new external optimizer baseline is introduced. Shampoo remains in NanoGPT, while its absence from the new GPT2 pretraining comparison is explained by memory constraints.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1000-step GPT2 pretraining with 512-token sequences, gradient accumulation, and warmup/cosine scheduling, plus two-epoch 774M-model fine-tuning with 128-token sequences and no warmup. Learning-rate sweeps and a shared Muon training trajectory for update-direction comparisons add evaluation procedures. Previously specified NanoGPT settings and hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: The original query/key ablation survives as Figure 6. V2 adds GPT2 learning-rate sensitivity analysis and a damping study comparing ASGO–Muon update-direction similarities across layers, damping choices, and SVD, Coupled Newton, and Newton–Schulz computations (Figures 2 and 7). These substantially extend robustness and numerical-behavior analysis.

E5.justification: V1 reports distributions across sampled learning rates but no repeated-seed confidence intervals. V2 introduces five different-seed runs and 95% confidence intervals for all fine-tuning comparisons in Table 6. This establishes a new uncertainty-reporting practice, without demonstrating an increase in runs for the retained NanoGPT experiments.

E6.justification: The NanoGPT curves and query/key findings are retained. New GPT2 validation losses are 3.87 for ASGO, 3.82 for Muon, 3.96 for AdamW, and 5.23 for DASGO (Table 1). In the new fine-tuning settings, DASGO has the lowest reported mean perplexity: 13.841 for causal modeling and 15.451 for fill-in-the-middle (Table 6). These are additional results under new conditions.

T1.justification: The principal convergence bounds remain unchanged. Proposition 1 changes from an epsilon-to-zero limit with a full-SVD proof to epsilon = 0 with a compact-SVD derivation, leaving singular-inverse handling implicit. Appendix F also doubles an intermediate epsilon term without changing the final theorem.

C1.justification: The empirical contribution broadens from Transformer pretraining to language-model tasks explicitly including fine-tuning. The central claims about ASGO's novelty, convergence advantages, structured-gradient exploitation, and unified handling of one-dimensional parameters remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of learning-rate robustness and damping sensitivity, including effects on small singular values and numerical instability in embedding layers. It explicitly identifies computational cost relative to Adam as a limitation and drops v1's suggestion of using DASGO as a warmup optimizer. These substantially expand the applicability and failure-condition discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds V100 hardware information, NanoGPT batch/epoch details, extensive settings and hyperparameter tables for the new experiments, and matrix-inverse implementation details. The NanoGPT additions are disclosures, not established setting changes. Reproducibility remains limited by conflicting GPT2 ASGO damping values: 10^-6 in Table 4 versus zero in Appendix C.3.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on modular optimization, SignSGD failures, block Fisher methods, GPT2, fill-in-the-middle training, and matrix functions. It also corrects the descriptions of Shampoo, KFAC, and TNT in Section 2. Positioning relative to concurrent One-Sided Shampoo remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 extensively reorganizes the narrative: notation and problem settings are merged, much related work and practical algorithm discussion move into Appendices A–B, and the query/key ablation moves into Appendix C. Theory commentary and the conclusion are rewritten, and Yi Ren is added to the author list.

P2.justification: V2 relocates the retained NanoGPT and query/key plots, separately redisplays NanoGPT validation loss in the main text, and adds GPT2 plots, damping panels, and performance/settings tables. V1's cited MLP-Hessian illustration is removed, while a cited block-spectra distance figure is added. Display organization changes substantially.

improvement.justification: V1's practical validation is confined to NanoGPT/Shakespeare. V2 substantially strengthens it through OpenWebText pretraining, two GPT2-Large fine-tuning objectives, repeated-seed confidence intervals, and targeted robustness diagnostics. These address an important limitation of the earlier evidence. Conflicting damping disclosures and less explicit singular-matrix handling in the revised equivalence proof introduce local clarity problems, but the broader, more informative empirical validation provides a substantial net improvement.
